Question: Having a new species require at least 2 mutated species (male and female) with same characteristics, and they need to be around the same area to have any chance of mating. If it is that difficult, how are there so many species on earth today?
Answer: What you're referring to is saltationism (from the Latin term for jump), sometimes referred to a little more colorfully as the hopeful monster hypothesis. The idea was that large macromutations create new species in a single blow. But, as the colorful name and your question point out, how would such hopeful monsters find partners to mate with? This idea did have some proponents back in the late 1800s and early 1900s, but the incorporation of genetics into evolutionary theory and the Modern Synthesis caused the idea to be mostly abandoned, at least for sexually reproducing animals. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. Populations already have genetic diversity. It's why no two individuals look exactly alike. And genetic mutation is decently common. In us humans, for example, it seems that pretty much everybody has a handful of new mutations*. But this genetic diversity doesn't keep us (or other populations of animals) from mating. And the new mutations that do creep into the population don't instantly create new species. They just add to the existing genetic diversity. For a population to split into two species takes time and isolation. The population somehow gets split into two separate populations, let's say Population A and Population B, that can't or don't mate with each other. These constant mutations will continue to spontaneously arise in each population, but they'll be limited to their respective populations. Mutations that arise in Population A, for example, can mix into that population over generations as all those animals mate with each other, but as long as Population B remains isolated from Population A, those mutations won't jump over to Population B. They'll be limited to Population A. And the same goes vice versa for new mutations that arise in Population B. Over time, as each of these population acquires more and more different mutations, they'll become more and more distinct from each other. Eventually, they'll have become different enough to be new species, but it's still a gradual process, with no stark dividing line. ABOVE SOURCE: Islands of speciation and speciation on islands This also explains why species is such a fuzzy boundary, with 'lumpers' and 'splitters' often disagreeing on whether different populations should be separate species, or merely subspecies. For example, a single study from 2020 , showed that there could be anywhere from 2 to 6 different species of giraffe depending on which specific criteria you used to define species. But sexually reproducing animals aren't the only organisms out there. Many types of animals are hermaphrodites, with male and female reproductive organs on the same individual. Many plants also produce male and female reproductive organs (stamens and pistils) on the same plant. If one of these types of organisms were to experience a substantial mutation, then it could potentially create a new species with that individual. In fact, this actually has been observed decently often for plants (take a look at section 5.1 of this page, Observed Instances of Speciation). Another exception is animals that reproduce by parthenogenesis, which is just a fancy term to describe animals where an egg can develop without being fertilized by a male. A notable recent case is the marbled crayfish. Their ancestral species is the slough crayfish from Georgia and Florida. People captured slough crayfish for pets, which led to captive breeding to supply the pet trade. Some time around the mid '90s, somebody in Germany discovered the new species, marbled crayfish, which can reproduce parthenogenetically. This new species like arose from a mutation in a single individual. (You might also see these animals referred to by their German name, marmokrebs.) So, your intuition was partially right about sexually reproducing animals. Even if there were massive mutations that would create a new species in a single individual, the odds of such mutations happening simultaneously to create a male and female of that new species are so astronomically low as to be effectively impossible. But, that’s not the way speciation actually occurs in sexually reproducing animals. It’s a gradual process among populations due the accumulation of many, many mutations. But among other types of organisms that can reproduce by themselves and so don’t have the problem of being hopeful monsters, then speciation can sometimes happen in a single individual. * The overall mutation rate is on the order of 100 - 200 mutations per person. But given that something like 90% of our genome is junk DNA, most of those mutations don't do much at all. Still, it seems that we do all get at least a handful of mutations to functional DNA. Question: If applying Occam's razor to the existence of God, wouldn't the most likely answer be that if 95 percent of people believe in God, then there is probably something to that claim?
Answer: It's not true that 95% of people believe in God. When referring to the capital G God in that manner, it's usually implied that you're referring to the God of Judaism and Christianity. Christians and Jews combined make up less than 1/3 of the world's population. You might possibly be lumping in Muslims in that group as the other major Abrahamic religion, though it's much more common to use the term Allah in reference to Islam. Still, even combining all of the Abrahamic religions, you get barely more than half of the world's population. Which means that just under half of the world's population don't believe in God, but rather in different gods or in no god at all. ABOVE SOURCE: Christians remain world’s largest religious group, but they are declining in Europe So if your argument is that majority beliefs should be a helpful tool in trying to figure out the truths about religion, let me point out that more than 2/3 of the people in the world are not Christians and don't believe in the Christian Trinity. Does that mean there is probably something to that claim?

Question: Americans: Tell me what you love so much about pumpkin pie. What makes it important for you?
Answer: Outside being traditional at certain holidays, it's not really "important", per se. It just tastes good. It's a great combination of a smooth texture from the filling with a crunchy texture from the crust, with a nice flavor without anything being overpowering or too intense, especially when you top it with a nice big dollop of whipped cream. ABOVE: A pumpkin pie with an appropriate amount of whipped cream SOURCE: Pumpkin Pie (Paula Deen) Recipe While I certainly like other pies, if you want to compare and contrast, pecan pies can often be too sweet – fine every once in a while, but it's hard to finish off an entire pie at Thanksgiving. Cherry pie is just too... cherry. Apple pie is very good, and we can polish off an entire apple pie at Thanksgiving, but I personally prefer the smoothness of a pumpkin pie to the fruity texture of the apples. Apple pie really needs to be accompanied with a healthy serving of ice cream or whipped cream to balance it out. Custard pies are great, but pumpkin pies are really just custard pies with added pumpkin flavor. Really, about the only pie I like more than pumpkin pie/custard pie is much more of a regional thing from where I grew up, and not so well known outside Pennsylvania Dutch Country – shoo fly pie. And I have to admit that even when I make shoo fly pie for gatherings here in Texas, most people seem to take a piece more out of politeness, and don't seem to love the pie the same way I do. ABOVE: Here's a bonus pic of shoo fly pie SOURCE: Shoofly Pie Recipe (and note, this is my favorite recipe, even more than my great grandmother’s recipe) So returning back to the question, pumpkin pie tastes great, and has a nice, pleasing, smooth texture balanced by a flaky crust.

Question: On what basis did evolutionists decide humans have a close common ancestry with apes, was it by looks? If so what about the kangaroo and the sloth? If by DNA, what about the banana? If it was by intelligence, what about the octopus?
Answer: Carl Linnaeus is known as the father of modern taxonomy. He developed the now traditional system that you probably learned in high school biology – Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. This system is a nested hierarchy that we now recognize as being due to evolutionary relatedness, but Linaeus himself was a creationist (he died before Darwin was even born), and was merely trying to recognize the pattern of God's creation. And he based his system largely on physical similarity. Of course, he went deeper than superficial resemblances, and looked at the entire anatomy of organisms. That is how, for example, he recognized that dolphins and whales were mammals and not fish. And Linnaeus recognized the obvious anatomical similarities between humans and other apes, putting humans, chimpanzees, and orangutans all in the same genus, Homo (gorillas weren't yet known to European naturalists, or he almost surely would have included them, as well). I mean, the similarities between humans and other apes is sometimes so striking it's almost eerie: ABOVE SOURCE: Bonobo photos by Frans de Waal Kangaroos and sloths aren't nearly so anatomically similar to humans as the other apes. I mean, yes they're both mammals, so they're more related to humans than, say, a magpie or an oak tree, but not at that same level of similarity as the other apes. I mean, kangaroos are marsupials, for heaven's sake, with many, may differences to us placental mammals. Linnaeus recognized this over 200 years ago. DNA wasn't recognized as our hereditary molecule until the 1940s, and it's only been in more recent decades that scientists have been able to sequence DNA and otherwise study it in much more detail. Much like the anatomical comparisons that Linnaeus pioneered, you can also compare the similarity of the DNA of different organisms, and construct nested hierarchies of similarity. And when scientists did this, the resulting 'trees' matched up nearly spot on with the trees developed from traditional classification. In other words, while we knew from anatomical comparisons that humans were more closely related to apes than to sloths, DNA studies found exactly the same thing. So you have two different lines of evidence to do these comparisons, yet they produce essentially the same results. You mentioned bananas. Bananas are only distantly related to us people, and the genetics confirms this. While our DNA is roughly 98% the same with chimpanzees (it depends on how exactly you're doing the comparison), it's only around 50% the same with bananas. But bananas are multicellular eukaryotes, so even they are more closely related to us than some other life forms. Bacteria, for example, are even more distant relatives, with even less DNA in common with us. Your last question is about intelligence. The thing about lots of evolutionary traits is that they can develop separately through convergent evolution. When this happens, although the traits might have superficial resemblance, there will be lots of differences in the details. And octopuses and other cephalopods have brains that are very different from us mammals. They developed their intelligence through a completely different evolutionary path than us. So yes, anatomical similarities and genetic similarities are both used to determine the relatedness of organisms. But intelligence is a trait that can evolve independently, so it’s not as useful on its own.

Name: Jeff Lewis
Question: If you have a Bible at hand, can you open it up to a random page and see what it says? Maybe it will change your life.
Answer: Okay. I decided to give this a try, and I really did open up to random pages rather than cherry picking verses that I knew were problematic just to make a point. And to up the odds that I’d get something good, I actually tried it three times, not just once. Here’s what I got: First Attempt – Joshua 14 and Joshua 15 Well, there's nothing really profound or life changing here. It was mostly just details of how the conquered areas of the Promised Land were divied out to the various Jewish people. Just to give a taste of how tedious it is: And their south boundary ran from the end of the Dead Sea, from the bay that faces southward; it goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, makes a turn to Karka, passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Wadi of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary. If you wanted to be less charitable, you could point out that the Israelites were the evil conquerors who went in and subjugated or displaced the people already living there, but that kind of thing is so common throughout history that it's just par for the course. I mean, look at how many times the lands that would become England were invaded and conquered by outsiders, or basically the entire history of Rome. (Also, somewhat thankfully, these stories about conquering the Promised Land probably aren’t true – Frans du Plessis's answer to Do we have extra-biblical evidence for the origins of the Israelites?) Second Attempt – 2 Chronicles 1 and 2 Chronicles 2 Well, at least we get one of the classic Bible stories, here, with God offering Solomon anything he wanted, and Solomon asking for wisdom. But it all reads as just typical ancient literature, so still nothing life changing. I'll note the the final couple verses, though: Then Solomon took a census of all the aliens who were residing in the land of Israel, after the census that his father David had taken, and there were found to be one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred. Seventy thousand of them he assigned as laborers, eighty thousand as stonecutters in the hill country, and three thousand six hundred as overseers to make the people work. Huh. No calls to send them back across the border where they came from, or complaints that the immigrants were stealing Israelite jobs. Just a pragmatic approach of putting them to work. I feel like there might be a lesson there for certain modern day folks who claim to follow the Bible. Third Attempt – Job 30 and Job 31 These were the chapters where Job wrapped up his defense to his friends who insisted that he must have done something wrong to have incurred God's wrath, while Job insisted that he'd done nothing wrong and had lived a good life. It's really just a reminder of how unfair and cruel God can be. As I've said elsewhere, the lesson one takes away from Job is that might makes right, and God is the mightiest of all. So I actually gave it three shots. None of the chapters I came across offered anything particularly profound or life changing. And actually, that is an important point that I don't think a lot of folks really understand. You so often hear people say that, even if you're not religious, at least the Bible is great literature, or carries profound moral lessons. But on the whole, it isn't, really. There may be certain sections of the Bible that are good (e.g. Ecclesiastes). But when you look at the entire Bible, it's a very mixed bag, with the tedious and mundane parts outnumbering the good parts.
